143	S: Soft tissues are mostly water, differ from water by less than 10 percent in how strongly they attenuate X-rays, and at CT energies about nine out of ten of their interactions with X-ray photons are Compton scattering.
144	V: 90 [percent of interactions in water at 70 keV that are Compton scattering] R: Water at 70 keV: about 90% Compton scatter, 5.4% Rayleigh scatter, 4.7% photoelectric absorption. Muscle and soft tissue are about 4.3 to 5.3% above water in mu; fat is about 7.9% below.
145	SRC: https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/Xcom/xcom2?Method=Comp&Output2=Hand , https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/Xcom/xcom2?Method=Mix&Output2=Hand , https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/tissue.html , https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/muscle.html , https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/adipose.html , https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1564webNew-74666420.pdf
146	N: Draft confirmed and quantified from NIST XCOM (see tables.interactions). mu at 70 keV: water 0.1937, muscle 0.202, soft tissue 0.204, fat 0.1785 per cm. This small spread (under 10 percent, that is a few tens of HU) is the reason CT needs precise measurements to tell soft tissues apart. At 511 keV more than 99 percent of interactions in water, soft tissue and bone are Compton scattering.
147	
148	### three-fates-of-an-x-ray-photon | Claim 8: what can happen to one X-ray photon in the body
149	S: Each X-ray photon entering the body does one of three things: it passes straight through and reaches the detector, it is absorbed by an atom and disappears (the photoelectric effect), or it bounces off an electron in a new direction (scattering).
150	V: three outcomes: transmitted, absorbed, scattered [] R: Two kinds of scattering occur at CT energies: Compton scattering (the photon gives part of its energy to an electron; about 90% of interactions in water at 70 keV) and Rayleigh scattering (the photon changes direction and keeps its energy; about 5.4%). A scattered photon can go on to scatter again, be absorbed, or leave the body.
151	SRC: https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1564webNew-74666420.pdf , https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/Xcom/xcom2?Method=Comp&Output2=Hand
152	N: Draft confirmed; Rayleigh (coherent) scattering added as a minor second kind of scatter so the site does not imply Compton is the only one. IAEA handbook chapter 2: photoelectric effect ("The incident photon disappears in the photoelectric interaction"), coherent (Rayleigh) scattering, Compton scattering; a scattered photon may "be followed by a third scatter, photoelectric absorption or no further interactions". Pair production needs at least 1022 keV, so it plays no part in CT or PET. The image is formed from the photons that pass straight through; scattered photons that still reach the detector add haze, which the anti-scatter grid on the detector reduces. "Bounces off an electron" is a simplification that fits Compton scattering; Rayleigh scattering involves the atom as a whole.
153	
154	### photons-do-not-slow-down | Claim 8: attenuation means fewer photons, not slower ones
155	S: X-ray photons do not slow down in the body; they all travel at the speed of light, and tissue only reduces how many of them arrive, which is what attenuation means.
156	V: speed unchanged; number reduced [] R: A Compton-scattered photon does lose energy, but it still travels at the speed of light: a 70 keV photon scattered through 90 degrees leaves with about 61.6 keV, and a 511 keV photon with about 256 keV.
157	SRC: https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1564webNew-74666420.pdf
158	N: Draft confirmed. The Beer-Lambert law (IAEA Eq. 11.1) is a statement about the number (intensity) of unscattered photons. Lower photon energy means longer wavelength, not lower speed. The speed statement is standard physics rather than a sentence quoted from the handbook; for X-rays the refractive index of tissue differs from 1 by a few parts per million or less, so "at the speed of light" is accurate for the site. Compton energies computed from E_after = E / (1 + (E / 511 keV) x (1 - cos angle)): 70 keV gives 61.6 keV at 90 degrees and 54.9 keV at 180 degrees; 511 keV gives 256 keV and 170 keV. GAME NOTE: if the site game shows photons slowing down in dense tissue, it should say plainly that this is a visual stand-in for "fewer photons get through", and that real photons never slow.
159	
160	### radon-transform | Claim 9: image reconstruction, the Radon transform
161	S: The mathematics behind CT goes back to 1917, when the mathematician Johann Radon showed that a two-dimensional pattern can be recovered from the sums measured along all the straight lines crossing it; the set of those line sums is now called the Radon transform.
162	V: 1917 [year] R: Radon's paper was not known to the people who built CT: Allan Cormack solved the problem independently, published in 1963 and 1964, and wrote that he learned of Radon's work only in the early 1970s.
163	SRC: https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/cormack-lecture.pdf , https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1979/press-release/ , https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1564webNew-74666420.pdf
164	N: Draft confirmed. Cormack Nobel lecture (1979): "Only then [the early seventies] did I learn of Radon's work on the line integral problem", reference 3: Radon, J., Ber. Sachs. Akad. Wiss. 69, 262 (1917); "Radon provided an affirmative answer and a formula". Nobel press release 1979: Cormack "published his analysis of the problem in two scientific publications in 1963 and 1964" and "was not aware then that the key mathematical problems had been considered earlier". IAEA handbook section 11.4.2 uses "Radon space" and "2-D Radon transform" for CT projection data. Radon's first name and nationality (Johann, Austrian) are from general knowledge; the lecture gives only "Radon, J. H.", so the name should be checked by the history batch and the nationality is left out. The range text says "not known to the people who built CT", which is supported for Cormack; Hounsfield's lecture does not mention Radon.
165	
166	### filtered-back-projection | Claim 9: image reconstruction, filtered back-projection
167	S: For about four decades the standard way to turn the measurements into a picture was filtered back-projection: each measured profile is sharpened with a "ramp" filter and then smeared back across the image along the direction it was measured from, and the smears from all angles add up to the cross-section.
168	V: about 40 [years as the standard method] R: Without the filter step, simple back-projection gives a strongly blurred image. The ramp filter is also called the Ram-Lak (Ramachandran-Lakshminarayanan) filter; scanners offer modified versions tuned for soft tissue or bone.
169	SRC: https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1564webNew-74666420.pdf , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9968777/ , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6443602/
170	N: Draft confirmed. Koetzier et al. 2023 (Radiology 306:e221257): "Filtered back projection (FBP) has been the standard CT image reconstruction method for 4 decades." Willemink and Noel 2019 (Eur Radiol 29:2185-95): "FBP was the method of choice for decades". IAEA handbook section 11.4: simple back-projection "yields a strongly blurred image"; the filter is "a ramp filter in the frequency domain ... Ramachandran-Lakshminarayanan filter, also called the Ram-Lak or ramp filter". "Sharpened" is plain-language for a filter that boosts fine detail (high spatial frequencies).
171	
172	### first-ct-used-iterative-reconstruction | Claim 9: image reconstruction, history
173	S: The first CT scanners of the early 1970s built their images with a step-by-step (iterative) method, but the computers of the time were too slow for it and filtered back-projection soon replaced it.
174	V: early 1970s [] R: The first clinical scan took about 5 minutes to acquire and about as long to reconstruct, at 80 x 80 pixels; most CT images today are 512 x 512 pixels.
175	SRC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6443602/
176	N: ADDED nuance: the draft says FBP "was the standard method for decades", which is true, but it was not the original method. Willemink and Noel 2019: "The first CT scanners in the early 1970s already used iterative reconstruction algorithms"; "Originally, CT images were reconstructed with an iterative method called algebraic reconstruction technique (ART). Due to lack of computational power, this technique was quickly replaced by simple analytic methods such as filtered back projection"; "The first clinical CT scan took about 5 min, and image reconstruction took approximately the same time ... only 80 x 80 pixels"; "512 x 512 pixels for most clinical applications". Scan and reconstruction times for the first scanner differ between accounts; the history batch should own those numbers.
177	
178	### iterative-reconstruction-return | Claim 9: image reconstruction, iterative methods
179	S: Since about 2009, faster computers have let scanner makers bring back iterative reconstruction, which repeatedly adjusts the image until it agrees with the measurements and gives cleaner pictures at lower radiation dose; it is now common.
180	V: 2009 [year (approximate start of routine clinical use)] R: Within a few years of 2009 all major CT makers offered iterative reconstruction. Types range from "hybrid" methods that mainly reduce noise to full model-based methods.
181	SRC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6443602/ , https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1564webNew-74666420.pdf , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9968777/
182	N: Draft confirmed. Willemink and Noel 2019: "it took until 2009 for the first iterative reconstruction algorithms to come commercially available"; "In 2009, the first IR algorithm called IRIS (iterative reconstruction in image space, Siemens Healthineers) received FDA clearance"; "Within a few years, all major CT vendors introduced IR algorithms". DOUBT on the "first": other accounts date GE's ASiR to 2008, which I did not verify; the statement therefore says "since about 2009" and names no first product. IAEA handbook (2014): "Iterative (statistical) reconstructions are now commonly used in CT."
183	
184	### deep-learning-reconstruction | Claim 9: image reconstruction, deep learning
185	S: The newest method, deep-learning reconstruction, uses a neural network trained on pairs of lower-quality and higher-quality scans to produce low-noise images; the first such products for CT were cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2019.
186	V: 2019 [year of first FDA clearances] R: By early 2023, three CT makers (GE, Canon, Philips) and two independent software companies had FDA-cleared deep-learning products.
187	SRC: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9968777/
188	N: Draft confirmed and dated. Koetzier et al. 2023: "In 2019, TrueFidelity (GE Healthcare) became the first DLR technique approved by the FDA"; "The second DLR algorithm approved by the FDA was ... AiCE, Canon Medical Systems ... in 2019"; Philips Precise Image in 2022; two image-denoising products (ClariCT.AI, PixelShine) cleared in 2019. The statement says "the first such products ... in 2019", which is true whichever product is counted first. The review writes "approved"; the regulatory term for these devices is "cleared". The review abstract, as returned by search, also reports dose reductions of up to 71 percent in selected studies; I did not check that figure in the full text, so it is left out of the statement.
189	
190	### ct-based-attenuation-correction | Claim 10: CT-based attenuation correction in PET/CT
191	S: In a PET/CT scanner the CT image does a second job: it is converted into a map of how strongly each part of the body attenuates 511 keV photons, and that map is used to correct the PET data for the photon pairs that were absorbed or scattered inside the patient.
192	V: attenuation correction [] R: Before PET/CT, the map came from a separate, lengthy transmission scan with radioactive sources; replacing it with CT cut whole-body scan time by up to 40 percent and gave a nearly noise-free map.
193	SRC: https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/45/1_suppl/4S.full.pdf , https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=12931319&rettype=abstract&retmode=text , https://tech.snmjournals.org/content/33/3/156 , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4315529/
194	N: Draft confirmed. Townsend et al. 2004: "the use of CT images for attenuation correction of the PET emission data, eliminating the need for a separate, lengthy PET transmission scan ... not only reduces whole-body scan times by up to 40% but also provides essentially noiseless ACFs". Kinahan et al. 2003 (Semin Nucl Med 33:166-79) abstract: transmission methods use "positron sources, gamma-ray sources, or x-ray sources"; error sources for the CT method are breathing mismatch between CT and PET, contrast agents, metal implants, and arms in the field of view. The EANM FDG PET/CT guideline (Boellaard 2015) recommends looking at images with and without attenuation correction to spot CT-caused artifacts.
195	
196	### ct-to-511-kev-conversion | Claim 10: converting CT numbers to 511 keV attenuation
197	S: Because CT measures attenuation at about 70 keV and PET needs it at 511 keV, the scanner rescales every pixel, using one straight-line conversion for air, lung and soft tissue and a second, less steep line for bone.
198	V: mu(511 keV) = 9.6e-5 x (HU + 1000) per cm below about 50 HU [per cm] R: This two-line ("bilinear") conversion gives 0.096 per cm for water (0 HU) and 0 for air (-1000 HU). Above the break point the slope is smaller and depends on the CT tube voltage. The ratio mu(511 keV)/mu(70 keV) is about 0.5 for water and about 0.35 for dense bone.
199	SRC: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=16696474&rettype=abstract&retmode=text , https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=12111133&rettype=abstract&retmode=text , https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/45/1_suppl/4S.full.pdf , https://tech.snmjournals.org/content/33/3/156 , https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/water.html , https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/bone.html
200	N: Draft confirmed with one correction of attribution (see kinahan-1998-reference): the bilinear method is described by Burger et al. 2002 for the GE Discovery LS ("uses a bilinear function based on the attenuation of water and cortical bone at the CT and PET energies") and by Carney et al. 2006 ("9.6 x 10(-5) (HU + 1000) below a threshold of approximately 50 HU and a(HU + 1000) + b above the threshold, where a and b are fixed parameters that depend on the kVp setting"). Break points and slopes differ between manufacturers. Check: Carney's line gives 0.0248 per cm for the inflated-lung row (HU -742), against 0.0247 computed from NIST. Scale ratios computed from NIST XCOM: water 0.09598/0.1929 = 0.498; cortical bone 0.08938/0.2570 = 0.348. Contrast agents and metal upset the conversion because they are bright on CT for a reason (high atomic number) that matters little at 511 keV.
201	
202	### kinahan-1998-reference | Claim 10: key reference, Kinahan et al. 1998
203	S: A 1998 paper in the journal Medical Physics by Paul Kinahan, David Townsend, Thomas Beyer and Donald Sashin showed, using CT and PET scans of test objects and of people, that a CT image can be used to correct PET data for attenuation in a combined PET/CT scanner.
204	V: Kinahan PE, Townsend DW, Beyer T, Sashin D. Attenuation correction for a combined 3D PET/CT scanner. Med Phys. 1998;25(10):2046-2053. doi:10.1118/1.598392 [] R: Published October 1998; PubMed ID 9800714. The data came from separate CT and PET scanners, with the images aligned by software.
205	SRC: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=9800714&rettype=abstract&retmode=text , https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/45/1_suppl/4S.full.pdf
206	N: Reference CONFIRMED (authors, journal, year, volume 25, issue 10, pages 2046-53, DOI). CORRECTION to the draft: this paper did not propose "bilinear scaling". Its abstract compares three methods, "segmentation, scaling, and our proposed hybrid segmentation/scaling method", for converting "from an effective CT photon energy of 70 keV to the PET photon energy of 511 keV"; in the hybrid method a threshold separates bone from non-bone and each gets its own scale factor (Townsend 2004). The bilinear function used on later scanners is a close relative (Burger 2002, Carney 2006). First-author affiliation in PubMed: Department of Radiology, University of Pittsburgh. The abstract calls the work a "proof of principle" and concludes "using CT information is a feasible way to obtain attenuation correction factors for 3D PET". The statement avoids the word "first": X-ray-based attenuation correction had been explored earlier for SPECT/CT, and I did not check priority.
207	
208	### pet-without-attenuation-correction | Claim 10: what an uncorrected PET image looks like
209	S: Without attenuation correction a PET image is misleading in a recognizable way: the skin and the lungs look too bright, and the deep center of the body looks too dim.
210	V: skin and lungs falsely bright; deep tissue falsely dim [] R: The error grows with body size. Doctors still look at the uncorrected images as a cross-check, because problems in the CT (metal, contrast agent, breathing mismatch) can create false bright spots in the corrected ones.
211	SRC: https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/44/11/1855.full.pdf , https://tech.snmjournals.org/content/33/3/156 , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4315529/
212	N: Draft confirmed. Bai, Kinahan et al. 2003 (J Nucl Med 44:1855-61): an image reconstructed without attenuation correction "illustrates the well-known artifacts of elevated tracer concentration in the lungs and skin"; in uniform regions such as the abdomen only "central regions of lower, or even negative, tracer concentration" are consistent with the uncorrected data; "The well-known disadvantages of not performing attenuation correction are the inaccuracies in the uptake, shape, and location of lesions". Reason: photon pairs from deep in the body must cross more tissue, so fewer are detected; pairs from the skin, and pairs crossing the low-density lungs, are lost less. Sureshbabu and Mawlawi 2005 (J Nucl Med Technol 33:156-61) and the EANM guideline (Boellaard 2015) describe using non-corrected images to check for CT-caused artifacts. "The error grows with body size" follows from the exponential law (see photon-pair-loss-in-the-body) and is not a quoted sentence.
213	
214	### photon-pair-loss-in-the-body | Claim 10: size of the attenuation effect at 511 keV
215	S: A PET event is counted only if both 511 keV photons escape the body, and along a line through 30 cm of tissue only about 1 pair in 18 does, so the correction is large.
216	V: 5.6 [percent of photon pairs surviving a 30 cm path in water] R: Survival for a total path in water of 10 / 20 / 30 / 40 cm: 38.3 / 14.7 / 5.62 / 2.15 percent (correction factors 2.61 / 6.82 / 17.8 / 46.5). The loss depends on the total tissue thickness along the line, not on where along the line the pair started.
217	SRC: https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/water.html , https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=12111133&rettype=abstract&retmode=text , https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/44/11/1855.full.pdf
218	N: Computed here, not quoted: pair survival = exp(-mu x D) with mu(water, 511 keV) = 0.09597 per cm and D the total path length through the body along the line joining the two detectors (each photon survives with probability exp(-mu x its own path), and the two paths add up to D). 30 cm: exp(-0.09597 x 30) = 0.0562, that is 1 in 17.8. Real bodies are not pure water (lungs attenuate less, bone more), and 30 cm is an illustrative adult torso width. This is added background for the site text; the draft did not include a number.

214	### photon-pair-loss-in-the-body | Claim 10: size of the attenuation effect at 511 keV
215	S: A PET event is counted only if both 511 keV photons escape the body, and along a line through 30 cm of tissue only about 1 pair in 18 does, so the correction is large.
216	V: 5.6 [percent of photon pairs surviving a 30 cm path in water] R: Survival for a total path in water of 10 / 20 / 30 / 40 cm: 38.3 / 14.7 / 5.62 / 2.15 percent (correction factors 2.61 / 6.82 / 17.8 / 46.5). The loss depends on the total tissue thickness along the line, not on where along the line the pair started.
217	SRC: https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/ComTab/water.html , https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=12111133&rettype=abstract&retmode=text , https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/44/11/1855.full.pdf
218	N: Computed here, not quoted: pair survival = exp(-mu x D) with mu(water, 511 keV) = 0.09597 per cm and D the total path length through the body along the line joining the two detectors (each photon survives with probability exp(-mu x its own path), and the two paths add up to D). 30 cm: exp(-0.09597 x 30) = 0.0562, that is 1 in 17.8. Real bodies are not pure water (lungs attenuate less, bone more), and 30 cm is an illustrative adult torso width. This is added background for the site text; the draft did not include a number.

 NIST: X-Ray Mass Attenuation Coefficients - Section 2 
 X-Ray Mass Attenuation Coefficients
 2. The Mass Attenuation Coefficient, μ / ρ 
A narrow beam of monoenergetic photons with an incident intensity 
 I o , penetrating a layer of material with mass thickness 
 x and density ρ , emerges 
with intensity I given by the exponential attenuation law
 (eq 1) 
Equation (1) can be rewritten as
 (eq 2) 
from which μ / ρ can be 
obtained from measured values of I o , I and x . 
Note that the mass thickness is defined as the mass per unit area, and is 
obtained by multiplying the thickness t by the density ρ , i.e., x = ρ t .
The various experimental arrangements and techniques from which 
 μ / ρ can be obtained, 
particularly in the crystallographic photon energy/wavelength regime, have 
recently been examined and assessed by Creagh and 
Hubbell (1987, 1990) as part of the International Union of Crystallography 
(IUCr) X-Ray Attenuation Project. This has led to new tables of 
 μ / ρ in the 1992 
 International Tables for Crystallography 
( Creagh and Hubbell, 1992). The current status of 
 μ / ρ measurements has also been
reviewed recently by Gerward (1993), and an updated 
bibliography of measured data is available in 
 Hubbell (1994). 
Present tabulations of μ / ρ 
rely heavily on theoretical values for the total cross section per atom, 
 σ tot , which is related to 
 μ / ρ according to
 (eq 3) 
In (eq 3), 
 u (= 1.660 540 2 × 10 -24 g 
 Cohen and Taylor 1986 ) is the atomic mass unit 
(1/12 of the mass of an atom of the nuclide 12 C), A is the 
relative atomic mass of the target element, and
